question: What is content negotiation in Spring MVC?
title: Content Negotiation in Spring MVC — Accept and Content-Type Headers
direct_answer: In Spring MVC, content negotiation selects a representation for the response, usually from the request's Accept header, the mapping's produces condition, and available HttpMessageConverters. Request Content-Type is a separate concern: it describes the body the client sent and is matched by consumes. The server does not have to support every format requested by the client.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of HTTP content negotiation mechanism and how Spring MVC implements it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Content-Type (request body format) with Accept (desired response format) or thinking Spring always returns JSON automatically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain both directions: Accept controls response format, Content-Type describes request body format, and show how Spring uses HttpMessageConverter to bridge them

sections.title: Content Negotiation Selects a Response Representation
sections.content:
Negotiation uses media types, not file extensions by default in modern Spring MVC. The Accept header can list several types with quality values. A mapping can narrow the options with produces, and the return value's Java type must be writable by a configured converter.

For request input, consumes and Content-Type perform the parallel selection. A method that consumes application/json is not eligible for a text/plain body even if its response can be JSON. Keep the two directions separate when diagnosing 406 and 415 responses.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Accept describes response media types the client can accept.
produces restricts what a handler can return; converters must be able to write it.
Content-Type describes the request body and is checked against consumes.
No acceptable response representation normally produces 406; unsupported request media type normally produces 415.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A client can send JSON and request XML in the same call: Content-Type: application/json describes the incoming body, while Accept: application/xml describes the preferred response. Spring first selects a matching handler, then chooses an HttpMessageConverter that can write the return value in an acceptable type. If the application has a JSON converter only, an XML-only Accept header cannot be satisfied. Calling this an agreement about all data exchanged hides the important request/response distinction.

sections.title: Content Negotiation at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Content negotiation|~Agree on the format|client + server|via HTTP headers|JSON, XML, etc.
blue|Accept header|~What the client wants|Accept: application/json|server picks a converter|drives response type
emerald|Spring's role|~Strategy + converters|matches Accept to converter|first supported wins|auto-configured
rose|Trap|~No matching converter|returns 406|add the format dependency|JSON is the Boot default

sections.title: Content Negotiation with Multiple Formats
When Content Negotiation Matters
sections.content: Use content negotiation when you're building a public REST API that serves multiple client types. A web browser might prefer HTML, a mobile app wants JSON, and an enterprise system needs XML. Without negotiation, you'd need three separate endpoints. It's also critical when you expose the same data model to legacy systems (XML) and modern frontends (JSON). In microservices, negotiation lets you add CSV export endpoints without changing existing JSON contracts. For internal-only APIs with a single client, you can skip negotiation and just return JSON everywhere — but knowing how it works shows you understand HTTP fundamentals.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mixing up Accept and Content-Type**: Freshers often think Content-Type controls both request and response. Accept is what the client wants back; Content-Type describes what the client is sending. Sending Accept: application/xml but reading Content-Type in code leads to bugs.
- **Assuming JSON is always default**: If Jackson isn't on the classpath or no converter is registered, Spring won't return JSON. You'll get 406 errors. Always check spring-boot-starter-web includes Jackson.
- **Ignoring 406 responses**: When you see 406 Not Acceptable in Postman, it means the Accept header doesn't match any produces value. Freshers debug the controller logic instead of checking the HTTP headers first.

seo.metaDescription: Learn content negotiation in Spring MVC — Accept vs Content-Type headers, HttpMessageConverter selection, JSON vs XML, 406 and 415 status codes.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: Content negotiation is the HTTP handshake where the client says what format it wants and the server decides if it can deliver.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: Content negotiation is the process where a client and server agree on the data format. The client sends an Accept header saying what format it wants in the response. Spring looks through its registered HttpMessageConverters to find one that can produce that format.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: There are two directions to this. The Accept header controls what format comes back in the response — the server selects a converter to serialize the output. The Content-Type header describes what format the client is sending in the request body — the server selects a converter to deserialize the input.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Accept: application/json: client wants JSON back — Spring uses Jackson.
Accept: application/xml: client wants XML — Spring needs jackson-dataformat-xml.
Content-Type: application/json: client is sending JSON — Jackson deserializes it.
406 Not Acceptable: no registered converter can produce the requested format.
415 Unsupported Media Type: no registered converter can read the incoming Content-Type.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: If the client doesn't send an Accept header, Spring defaults to JSON when Jackson is configured. Many developers don't know content negotiation is even happening because JSON just works by default. The mechanism only becomes visible when clients request a different format or send an unsupported Content-Type.

speakable_v2.cap: Use the produces attribute on your mapping annotations to explicitly declare what formats an endpoint supports, rather than relying on global negotiation silently.

question: What is the produces attribute in @GetMapping?
title: produces Attribute in @GetMapping — Restricting Response Content Type
direct_answer: The produces attribute declares which response media types a handler method can produce. Spring includes it in request mapping and compares it with the request's Accept preferences during handler selection. If no selected handler can produce an acceptable representation, MVC normally returns 406 Not Acceptable. The value can be a media-type string or a constant whose value is that string.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of endpoint-level content type constraints and how they interact with Accept headers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing produces exists or thinking Spring automatically supports all formats without configuration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both produces and consumes together on a POST endpoint to demonstrate understanding of bidirectional constraints

sections.title: The produces Mapping Condition
sections.content: Handler mapping and message conversion are related but separate. A produces condition can select a handler, then a converter serializes the returned Java value. Merely declaring application/xml does not install an XML serializer. Quality parameters and wildcards in Accept can influence negotiation, and absent Accept commonly behaves like */*.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: produces describes response representation types.
Accept describes what the client can receive.
The selected HttpMessageConverter must also be able to write the returned value.
Do not add produces=application/json when an endpoint genuinely supports negotiated formats.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, @GetMapping(value="/report", produces=MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE) matches a client accepting application/json. A client accepting only application/xml receives 406 unless another matching XML-producing method/converter is available. Writing produces="application/json" is equally valid because the annotation property is a String array.

sections.title: The produces Attribute
sections.content:
amber|produces|~Restricts output type|on @GetMapping|produces = APPLICATION_JSON|narrows the route
blue|Matching|~Against Accept header|client must accept it|else 406 Not Acceptable|content negotiation
emerald|Use for|~Multiple formats|JSON vs XML endpoints|same path, different produces|version via media type
rose|Trap|~Mismatch with Accept|gives 406|client sends wrong Accept|align both sides

sections.title: Using produces and consumes Together
When to Use produces
sections.content: Use produces when you want explicit control over response formats. If your API only supports JSON and you don't want to handle XML requests, add produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE to prevent 406 errors from being confusing. It's also useful when you have multiple endpoints serving the same resource in different formats — one for JSON at /api/user/123, another for CSV at /api/user/123/export with produces = text/csv. In versioned APIs, you can use custom media types like application/vnd.company.v2+json in produces to route to different controller methods based on version. For public APIs, produces documents what formats each endpoint supports, making it easier for clients to integrate. Skip produces if you're building an internal API where all consumers use JSON and you want Spring's default behavior.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using hardcoded strings instead of constants**: Writing produces = "application/json" instead of MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE. The constant prevents typos and makes refactoring easier.
- **Forgetting produces only filters GET/HEAD**: For POST endpoints, you need both consumes (for request body) and produces (for response). Freshers often set only produces and wonder why their POST fails with 415 when sending JSON.
- **Not understanding 406 vs 415**: 406 means the Accept header doesn't match produces. 415 means the Content-Type doesn't match consumes. Freshers see these status codes and think it's a Spring bug instead of a header mismatch.
- **Overly restrictive produces on all endpoints**: Setting produces on every endpoint when you only return JSON creates maintenance overhead. Use it selectively where you need format constraints.

question: How does Spring Boot auto-configure JSON support?
title: Spring Boot JSON Auto-Configuration — Jackson and ObjectMapper
direct_answer: When Jackson is on the classpath, Spring Boot can auto-configure a Jackson ObjectMapper and Spring MVC can register a Jackson HttpMessageConverter. That makes JSON a common representation, but it does not force every @RestController return value to application/json. Content negotiation, produces, the return type, and all configured converters determine the response.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot auto-configuration for JSON and how Jackson is integrated
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that spring-boot-starter-web already includes Jackson or trying to manually configure ObjectMapper without understanding auto-configuration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how to customize ObjectMapper with application.properties or a custom Bean to override defaults

sections.title: How Spring Boot Configures Jackson for MVC
sections.content:
Serialization has two layers. Boot creates/customizes Jackson objects; MVC chooses a message converter for a particular request and response. A custom ObjectMapper bean replaces Boot's default mapper, while Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer can adjust the auto-configured one without replacing it.

Inspect the selected Content-Type and converter when output is surprising. Avoid saying Boot simply sets JSON as the default for every RestController method, because a ResponseEntity<Resource>, plain text response, explicit produces value, or different Accept header follows different rules.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: JacksonAutoConfiguration supplies and customizes ObjectMapper infrastructure when conditions match.
Spring MVC's converter configuration makes that mapper usable for JSON bodies.
A user-defined ObjectMapper or converter can make auto-configuration back off or change behavior.
String, byte, resource, XML, and other response types can use other converters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The web starter commonly brings Jackson, so returning an OrderDto from a RestController with Accept: application/json is written by MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter. Boot applies Jackson properties and registered modules to its mapper. Returning a String may instead use StringHttpMessageConverter, and an XML converter can produce XML if installed and negotiated. JSON support is conditional infrastructure, not an annotation-level promise that every response is JSON.

sections.title: Spring Boot JSON Auto-Configuration
sections.content:
amber|JacksonAutoConfiguration|~Triggers on classpath|jackson-databind present|creates an ObjectMapper bean|zero config
blue|Converter|~MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter|registered automatically|JSON read + write|for all controllers
emerald|Customize|~Define an ObjectMapper bean|or application.properties|spring.jackson.*|dates, null handling
rose|Trap|~Two ObjectMappers|custom backs off default|@ConditionalOnMissingBean|don't duplicate

sections.title: Customizing Jackson ObjectMapper
When to Customize Jackson
sections.content: Use the default auto-configured ObjectMapper for most internal APIs where you control both client and server. Customize it when you need specific JSON formatting: snake_case field names for Python clients, excluding null fields to reduce payload size, or formatting dates as strings instead of timestamps for readability. If you're integrating with a legacy system that expects specific JSON structure, create a custom ObjectMapper bean. For APIs with strict JSON-LD or HAL requirements, register custom serializers. In microservices with shared DTOs, you might define a custom ObjectMapper in a shared library to ensure consistent JSON across all services. If you only need per-field customization, use Jackson annotations like @JsonProperty or @JsonFormat on your model classes instead of modifying the global ObjectMapper.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Manually adding Jackson dependency**: Freshers add jackson-databind to pom.xml when spring-boot-starter-web already includes it. This can cause version conflicts. Always check what your starter includes first.
- **Not understanding auto-configuration override**: Creating a Bean named objectMapper but not realizing Spring Boot's default is still active because they misspelled the method or used wrong scope. The custom bean must match the name and return type exactly.
- **Using @Autowired ObjectMapper in config**: Trying to inject ObjectMapper in the same @Configuration class that creates it causes circular dependencies. Define it as a @Bean method, don't inject it.
- **Ignoring application.properties**: Spring Boot lets you configure common ObjectMapper settings via properties like spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null. Freshers write a whole @Bean when a single property would work.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: When spring-boot-starter-web is on the classpath, Spring Boot's JacksonAutoConfiguration activates. It creates a default ObjectMapper bean, registers MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, and makes JSON the default response format for all @RestController methods.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: You can customize the ObjectMapper through application.properties without writing any code. Setting spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps=false makes dates serialize as ISO strings. Setting spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=NON_NULL skips null fields in every response.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: application.properties: configure global ObjectMapper behavior — indent output, date format, null handling.
@Bean ObjectMapper: define your own bean for full control — Spring Boot backs off and uses yours.
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer: add to the auto-configured settings without replacing them entirely.
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=true): on a DTO class — silently ignore unknown fields during deserialization.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: Defining an @Bean ObjectMapper replaces the entire auto-configured one. You lose any customizations Boot applied. For most cases, Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer is the safer choice — it applies on top of the auto-configuration rather than replacing it.

speakable_v2.cap: JavaTimeModule handles Java 8 LocalDate and LocalDateTime serialization. Spring Boot usually auto-registers it — verify by testing a date field in your response.

question: What is MediaType in Spring MVC?
title: MediaType in Spring MVC — Content Type Constants
direct_answer: MediaType is a Spring class containing constants for MIME type strings used in produces, consumes, and Content-Type headers. Key constants include APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE for application/json, APPLICATION_XML_VALUE, TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE, and MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE. Using these constants prevents typos and makes code more maintainable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of MediaType constants as best practice over hardcoded strings
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using hardcoded strings like application slash json instead of MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE everywhere
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention MediaType can be parsed, compared, and checked for compatibility using methods like isCompatibleWith

sections.title: MediaType: Type-Safe MIME Type Constants
sections.content:
**MediaType** is a Spring Framework utility class in the org.springframework.http package that provides constants for **MIME types** (also called media types or content types). Instead of writing the string "application/json" everywhere, you use **MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE**.

This prevents typos like "applicaton/json" that would cause 406 or 415 errors at runtime. MediaType has two forms: the constant itself (e.g. MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) which is a MediaType object, and the _VALUE suffix (e.g. MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE) which is the raw string "application/json". For annotations like @GetMapping(produces = ...), you use the _VALUE form because annotations require compile-time constants. The MediaType class also has methods for parsing media type strings, comparing types, and checking compatibility. For example, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON.isCompatibleWith(MediaType.ALL) returns true. This is useful when writing custom logic that needs to handle multiple formats. Using MediaType constants is a **Spring best practice** that improves code readability and catches errors at compile time.

sections.title: MediaType Constants
sections.content:
amber|MediaType|~MIME type constants|APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE|for produces/consumes|avoids typos
blue|_VALUE suffix|~String vs object|..._VALUE is the String|use in annotations|MediaType object elsewhere
emerald|Common ones|~JSON, XML, plain|APPLICATION_JSON|APPLICATION_XML|TEXT_PLAIN
rose|Trap|~Hardcoding strings|"aplication/json" typo|use the constant|compile-safe

sections.title: Using MediaType Constants in Controllers
When MediaType Constants Matter
sections.content: Use MediaType constants in every @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping annotation where you specify produces or consumes. This catches typos at compile time instead of runtime. When building file upload endpoints, use MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE. For file downloads, use MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE. If you're exposing CSV exports, use MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE or define custom types. In custom HttpMessageConverter implementations, use the MediaType object form to check compatibility: if (mediaType.isCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)) { ... }. For APIs that return different formats based on complex logic, parse the Accept header into MediaType objects and compare them programmatically. In tests, use MediaType constants in MockMvc: mockMvc.perform(get(...).accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)). This makes tests more readable and refactoring safer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using the wrong constant form**: Writing produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON (the object) instead of MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE (the string). Annotations need compile-time string constants, so you get a compilation error.
- **Hardcoding strings**: Writing produces = "application/json" everywhere. One typo like "applicaiton/json" breaks the endpoint at runtime with 406 errors. MediaType constants prevent this.
- **Not knowing common types**: Learners often don't know MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE exists for file uploads or MediaType.TEXT_HTML_VALUE for HTML responses. They hardcode these and wonder why their code looks inconsistent.
- **Ignoring isCompatibleWith**: When writing custom logic, Learners do string equality checks like mediaType.equals("application/json") instead of using MediaType's built-in compatibility methods that handle wildcards like application slash star.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **MediaType class**: Spring utility in org.springframework.http providing constants for MIME types
**_VALUE suffix**: string constant form used in annotations like APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE for produces and consumes
**Object form**: MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON is a MediaType object with methods for parsing and comparison
**Common constants**: APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, APPLICATION_XML_VALUE, TEXT_PLAIN_VALUE, MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE, APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE
**Compile-time safety**: using constants catches typos at compile time instead of runtime 406/415 errors

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: MediaType is a Spring class that holds constants for MIME types, which are the format strings like application slash json or text slash html. Instead of writing the string directly, I use MediaType dot APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE. The reason is it prevents typos. If I write 'application slash jason' by mistake, my endpoint returns 406 errors and it's hard to debug. With the constant, I get a compile error immediately if I mistype it. There are two forms of each constant. The one with _VALUE at the end like APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE is a string, and that's what I use in annotations like GetMapping produces. The one without _VALUE like APPLICATION_JSON is a MediaType object, and that has methods for comparing and checking compatibility. For example, if I'm writing custom logic that needs to check if a request is JSON, I can use isCompatibleWith to handle wildcards. Common constants I use are APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE for REST APIs, MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE for file uploads, and APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM_VALUE for binary file downloads. A mistake I've seen is people using the wrong form in annotations. They write produces equals MediaType dot APPLICATION_JSON without the _VALUE, and it doesn't compile because annotations need string literals. Using MediaType constants is just a best practice. It makes code more readable and safer because you're not scattering string literals everywhere. In a real project, every produces and consumes should use these constants.

beats.content: There are two forms to know. The VALUE variant — like APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE — is a plain String constant. Use it in annotation attributes like produces and consumes. The non-VALUE variant — like APPLICATION_JSON — is a MediaType object. Use it when calling methods that take a MediaType parameter, like HttpHeaders.setContentType.

beats.label: parts_or_states

APPLICATION_XML_VALUE: for XML responses.

question: What is the difference between Content-Type and Accept HTTP headers?
title: Content-Type vs Accept HTTP Headers — Request and Response Format
direct_answer: Content-Type describes the representation carried by the current message body. Accept lists response media types the client can accept. A request with an unsupported body Content-Type can produce 415, while an endpoint unable to produce any acceptable response type can produce 406. Not every request has a body, so Content-Type is not required on every call.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of HTTP content negotiation mechanics and request/response header directionality
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Content-Type as controlling response format or thinking Accept applies to the request body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the bidirectional nature: Content-Type flows with the body (request or response), Accept is a client preference declaration

sections.title: Content-Type and Accept Describe Opposite Directions
sections.content:
Spring uses consumes/produces mapping conditions and HttpMessageConverter capabilities. Missing Content-Type for a required body may cause a 415 or another binding outcome depending on the mapping and converters; it is not accurate to say every POST without it must fail. Security credentials and correlation ids are independent headers, not content negotiation.

**Example.** Content-Type: application/json describes the JSON being posted, while Accept: application/xml asks the server for an XML response.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Request Content-Type tells the server how to read the request body.
Request Accept tells the server what response forms are acceptable.
Response Content-Type tells the client what the returned body contains.
Set headers to match an actual body and documented negotiation contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, POST /orders with Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json says the request body is JSON and a JSON response is acceptable. If the endpoint consumes only JSON but receives text/plain, it can return 415. If it can write only JSON while the client accepts only application/xml, it can return 406.

sections.title: Content-Type vs Accept
sections.content:
amber|Content-Type|~Format of the body sent|on request and response|"this is what I'm sending"|drives @RequestBody read
blue|Accept|~Format client wants back|on the request|"send me this format"|drives the response converter
emerald|Together|~POST with both|Content-Type: json (body)|Accept: json (response)|full negotiation
rose|Trap|~Confusing the two|Content-Type for response|Accept for request body|keep directions straight

sections.title: Headers in Action with RestTemplate
When These Headers Matter
sections.content:
Use **Content-Type** when your request has a body (POST, PUT, PATCH)—without it, Spring can't deserialize your data and will return 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Use **Accept** when you need a specific response format from an API that supports multiple formats—if you omit it, the server picks a default (usually JSON in Spring Boot). In microservice communication, always set both: Content-Type ensures your service correctly interprets incoming data, Accept ensures you get responses in the format your service expects. When building a mobile app that prefers JSON and a web app that prefers HTML from the same backend, the Accept header lets each client get the right format without changing the server endpoint.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using Content-Type to request response format**: Freshers often think setting Content-Type: application/xml will make the server return XML. Content-Type only describes what you're sending, not what you want back—that's Accept's job.
- **Forgetting Content-Type on POST requests**: Sending JSON data without Content-Type: application/json causes 415 errors because Spring doesn't know how to parse the body. The header isn't optional when there's a body.
- **Expecting Accept to affect request parsing**: Setting Accept: application/xml doesn't change how Spring reads your request body—it only affects the response. If you send JSON, you still need Content-Type: application/json regardless of your Accept value.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Content-Type describes the format of the data being sent right now. The client sets it on a POST or PUT request body to say 'this is JSON I'm sending you'. The server sets it on the response to say 'this is JSON I'm sending back'.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: Accept is a preference declaration. The client sets it to say 'this is the format I want in your response'. The server uses it to pick the right serializer.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: In a typical POST: Content-Type: application/json tells Spring to deserialize the request body with Jackson. Accept: application/json tells Spring to serialize the response with Jackson. They often match, but they don't have to — a client could send XML and want JSON back.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: gotcha: If a client sends a POST with a JSON body but forgets to set Content-Type: application/json, Spring can't determine the format and may return 415 Unsupported Media Type. This is one of the most common mistakes when testing APIs with curl or Postman for the first time.

speakable_v2.cap: In Spring: consumes checks the incoming Content-Type. produces checks the incoming Accept header. The directions mirror the headers.
